messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Kiet, a 60-year-old hotel manager of Vietnamese descent, was overseeing a routine maintenance crew in the basement of his hotel when a contractor accidentally ruptured a line carrying a concentrated industrial solvent. The sharp, acrid chemical filled the small room; Kiet inhaled deeply before he could turn away. Within seconds his throat burned and clamped shut, his lungs seized, and he dropped to his knees, certain he was dying. He was rushed to the emergency room, treated for acute chemical pneumonitis, and discharged after three days with no lasting physical damage. The doctors said he was lucky. Kiet did not feel lucky.

In the weeks that followed, the memory of that taste—metallic, sweet, impossibly sharp—would force its way into his mind without warning, often while he was doing something as ordinary as checking inventory. The recollection was so vivid it brought the sensation back to his tongue, and in those moments he felt the room tilt and shrink around him, the panic of suffocation replaying in real time. These intrusions left him exhausted and convinced that his own body had become a trap. He had always been a capable man who solved problems; now he believed he could no longer trust his own body to keep him safe, and that no matter what he did, bad things could happen to him any time. At work he found himself growing quiet and isolated. The lobby smelled faintly of floor cleaner, and the scent would trigger a jolt of alarm—a false alarm, he knew intellectually, but his heart would race and his hands would tremble before he could stop it. He began to feel that he no longer belonged anywhere, not even in the hotel he had run for fifteen years.

Kiet started to scan every room he entered for signs of threat: a spilled container, an unfamiliar odor, a worker in a mask. His body stayed tense, always ready to react, and when something took longer than expected—a delayed delivery, a guest complaint that required extra steps—he immediately assumed a chemical leak or a dangerous situation was unfolding. His partner noticed he was jumpy and withdrawn, and if she or colleagues mentioned the incident, he would cut the conversation short or walk away, because being reminded of the event by others felt like a fresh exposure. Over time, these strategies became automatic. Whenever a memory surfaced—often triggered by the taste and smell of anything remotely chemical—he would check his own breathing, his skin, the tightness in his throat, searching for evidence that he was being poisoned again. That checking, in turn, brought the memory back more vividly, because focusing on his body made him feel the remembered burning sensation. He had come to believe that vigilance was the only thing standing between him and disaster, even though he also believed he was helpless to prevent it.

The cycle tightened. A false alarm—a whiff of bleach from a housekeeping cart—sent his body into alert, and that alertness triggered the memory of the basement, the taste, the terror. The memory confirmed that his body was unreliable and that he could not stop bad things from happening. This deepened his sense of alienation, which made him monitor his body even more frantically and avoid any context that might remind him. He stopped going to the basement entirely, delegating tasks, and began to feel like an imposter in his own hotel. What finally brought Kiet to seek help was a confrontation with his partner, who told him she felt she was living with a stranger—a man who was always scanning, always tense, never fully present. Kiet was afraid that if he stopped the monitoring, he would miss the next chemical leak and die. But he was equally afraid of losing the relationship that still anchored him. He came to therapy hoping to learn how to trust his body again, though he was not sure such a thing was possible.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Threat: No paragraph conveys that Negative Appraisals (e.g., 'body is a trap', 'bad things can happen anytime') causally lead to a sense of Threat; the threat is triggered by sensory cues, not by the appraisals themselves.
  e.g. "Having decided that she was permanently vulnerable, she walked into rooms already braced — the threat arrived with her before anything had happened."
  e.g. "The belief that she was a target — not unlucky, but chosen — meant that every unfamiliar face carried a weight of potential danger."
  e.g. "Her certainty that she couldn't protect herself made every new situation feel like a test she was already failing."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph conveys that Negative Appraisals causally lead to intrusive Memory; instead, Memory triggers Negative Appraisals, and Threat triggers Memory.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that a sense of Threat causally leads to Negative Appraisals; Threat leads to Memory, which then leads to Negative Appraisals, but not directly.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that Maladaptive Strategies (scanning, checking) causally lead to Negative Appraisals; while strategies reinforce cycles, the vignette does not show them directly causing distorted beliefs.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: No paragraph conveys that Maladaptive Strategies causally lead to an increased sense of Threat; strategies are responses to threat but are not shown to amplify the threat itself.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He had come to believe that vigilance was the only thing standing between him and disaster, even though he also believed he was helpless to prevent it.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Having decided that his body could no longer be trusted and that disaster was always one breath away, Kiet walked into every room already braced — the threat arrived with him before anything had actually happened.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
These intrusions left him exhausted and convinced that his own body had become a trap.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The conviction that he was permanently damaged and could not keep himself safe kept pulling him back to the basement, to that first burning inhalation, as if replaying it might finally reveal what he should have done differently.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
His body stayed tense, always ready to react, and when something took longer than expected—a delayed delivery, a guest complaint that required extra steps—he immediately assumed a chemical leak or a dangerous situation was unfolding.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Feeling this frightened all the time, Kiet had quietly come to accept what his body kept insisting on: that he was not the kind of person who got to feel safe anymore.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Whenever a memory surfaced—often triggered by the taste and smell of anything remotely chemical—he would check his own breathing, his skin, the tightness in his throat, searching for evidence that he was being poisoned again.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Each time he scanned his body for signs of danger and found none, the very act of checking confirmed he must be fragile enough to need it — otherwise he would have stopped by now.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
That checking, in turn, brought the memory back more vividly, because focusing on his body made him feel the remembered burning sensation.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
By never staying in a triggering environment long enough to discover it was actually safe, Kiet's nervous system had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as acute and urgent as the day it was set.
<<<END>>>
